newsitem.title: USA: U.S. grain stocks tight, focus turns to harvest.
newsitem.headline: U.S. grain stocks tight, focus turns to harvest.

text.p: The government on Monday pegged available grain stocks in the United States at historic low levels and the focus switched to the Midwestern corn and soybean harvests as the last chance this year to refill empty grain bins.

"Bad weather could still significantly hurt the crop," said Mike Hoover of the economic consulting firm, The WEFA Group. "The numbers that are going to make the difference now are the production numbers."

Despite the tight stocks projected, grain prices dropped sharply on commodity markets in reaction to favourable weather forecasts in the Midwest, where the soybean and corn harvests are accelerating, and some surprise that the Agriculture Department did not report even lower stocks.
Soybean futures contracts at the Chicago Board of Trade dropped as much as 25 cents a bushel, corn declined up to 8 cents and wheat lost as much as 5 cents a bushel.

"These stocks are very low numbers, but the market is reacting to the weather now," said Jerry Gidel, market analyst for Dean Witter Reynolds in Chicago. "The break in corn and soybeans was accentuated because of the good weather."

The Agriculture Department said that based on a survey of 50,000 farmers and 11,500 grain storage facilities across the nation during the first two weeks of September, corn supplies on Sept. 1 totalled around only 425 million bushels -- down more than 70 percent from the year-ago level of 1.6 billion bushels, and the lowest in 20 years.
Soybean stocks were estimated at 183 million bushels, down almost 50 percent from stocks on hand a year ago.

Available stocks of wheat, which have been replenished by the recently completed winter and spring wheat harvests, were pegged at 1.7 billion bushels, down only 8 percent from a year ago but still the lowest level in at least 10 years.
Commodity traders and agricultural analysts said weather in the next 6 weeks in the key Midwestern growing areas will be critical to begin the process of refilling depleted corn and soybean bins.

"The corn and soybean crops are as good as they're going to get right now," said WEFA's Hoover. "But the crop was put into the ground late, the growing season has been shortened and we're facing some early frost damage potential more so than other years."

The Agriculture Department is estimating U.S. corn production this year will recover from last year's small output and hit 8.8 billion bushels, which would be the fourth-largest corn crop on record. Soybean production is projected at almost 2.3 billion bushels, the second-largest crop ever.

Analysts said that every bit of the projected large harvests will be needed to meet demand by domestic users and foreign buyers. Any weather scare over the next few weeks will heat up the already nervous markets and cause crop prices to jump, they said.
"There's a lot of upside potential over the next month and a half, depending on what the weather does," said one.
However, some commodity experts noted that good crops outside the United States could somewhat temper any price hikes.

"Good global grain supplies should be available in the next several months," said an analyst with a major exporting company. "The price impact of the foreign crop is the big question mark -- you'll have tight stocks here but not elsewhere, so how much will that weigh on U.S. prices?"
